1.title: A client connects and says nothing
1.request: TCP connect to the port named by `-accept`; the client sends no bytes
1.response: Nothing on the wire. The socket stays open and the server waits for a ClientHello.
1.note: TLS is strictly client-speaks-first: the ClientHello is the first byte either side sends. A server that writes a greeting on accept, or that closes an idle socket immediately, fails this stage.

1.title: A client connects and disconnects without a ClientHello
1.request: TCP connect, then an immediate FIN
1.response: The server closes that socket and goes back to accepting. Nothing is logged as fatal and the process keeps running.
1.note: Port scanners and health checks do this all day. `read()` returning 0 before a ClientHello is the end of a connection, not an error to abort on.

14.response: They appear as extension types, cipher suites, named groups, signature schemes, versions and ALPN protocols. Skip them everywhere.

18.title: The schedule, top to bottom
18.request:
0 -> HKDF-Extract(salt=0, IKM=PSK|0) -> Early Secret
Early Secret -> Derive-Secret(., "derived", "") -> salt
salt + (EC)DHE -> HKDF-Extract -> Handshake Secret
Handshake Secret -> Derive-Secret(., "c hs traffic"|"s hs traffic", CH..SH)
Handshake Secret -> Derive-Secret(., "derived", "") -> salt
salt + 0 -> HKDF-Extract -> Master Secret
18.response: Master Secret -> Derive-Secret(., "c ap traffic"|"s ap traffic", CH..server Finished), "exp master" likewise, and "res master" over CH..client Finished.
18.note: Every arrow is one HMAC call. The two `"derived"` steps are over the hash of the empty string, and every other Derive-Secret is over the transcript so far.

18.title: HkdfLabel on the wire
18.response:
info = 00 10 | 09 | 74 6c 73 31 33 20 6b 65 79 | 00
that is: length 16, a 9-byte label "tls13 key", and a zero-length context.
18.note: Six bytes of prefix, and the sixth is a space. Getting that wrong gives keys that are self-consistent and interoperate with nothing.

19.title: Which hash is used where
19.request:
CH..SH                 -> client/server handshake traffic secrets
CH..Certificate        -> the CertificateVerify signature
CH..CertificateVerify  -> the server's Finished
CH..server Finished    -> the application traffic secrets and the client's Finished
CH..client Finished    -> resumption_master_secret
19.response: Five snapshots of one running hash, taken in order. Nothing is ever hashed twice and nothing is ever removed.
19.note: Take the snapshot before adding the message that consumes it. Adding the Finished and then computing its own verify_data is the classic off-by-one here, and it fails with an opaque 'bad Finished'.

19.title: What never goes in
19.request: Record headers; ChangeCipherSpec records; the AEAD tag and padding; the sequence numbers; anything read off the socket that is not a handshake message body
19.response: Only `msg_type || uint24 length || body`, in the order the messages were sent, reassembled across records where they were fragmented.
19.note: A handy check while building: hash the messages you *sent and received* at the message layer, never the bytes you read at the socket layer.

20.title: From a traffic secret to a record
20.request:
key = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret, "key", "", key_length)
iv  = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret, "iv",  "", 12)
nonce = iv XOR seq (right-aligned, 64-bit big-endian)
aad = the five record header bytes, ciphertext length included
20.response: ciphertext = AEAD-Encrypt(key, nonce, aad, content || content_type || zeros), and the record on the wire is `17 03 03 <len> <ciphertext||tag>`.
20.note: Four inputs, and three of them are derived rather than sent. The sequence number is the only state either side keeps, and it resets to zero whenever the keys change.

20.title: Key and IV lengths per suite
20.request:
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256: 16-byte key, 12-byte IV, 16-byte tag
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384: 32-byte key, 12-byte IV, 16-byte tag
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256: 32-byte key, 12-byte IV, 16-byte tag
20.response: Only the key length changes. The nonce is 12 bytes and the tag 16 bytes in every TLS 1.3 suite.
20.note: The hash changes too, and that is the bigger difference: SHA-384 makes every secret, transcript hash and finished key 48 bytes instead of 32.

23.title: The counter's whole life
23.request:
handshake keys installed -> 0
the client's Finished     -> 1
application keys installed -> 0
first application record   -> 1
KeyUpdate sent (under the old keys) -> 3, then new keys -> 0
23.response: The server counts its own writes the same way, independently. Nothing about either counter is ever transmitted.
23.note: The reset is the part that bites. A counter that keeps running across the key change gives every record after the handshake the wrong nonce, and the failure looks exactly like a wrong key.

23.title: Why out-of-order is not a special case
23.request: A record arrives twice, or two records arrive swapped
23.response: The second one is opened with the next nonce, which is not the nonce it was sealed with, so the tag does not verify: bad_record_mac(20), fatal.
23.note: TLS 1.3 does not need a replay window because the record layer is strictly ordered and the transport is TCP. There is nothing extra to implement.

26.title: Three schemes, three shapes
26.request:
ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 -> DER SEQUENCE { INTEGER r, INTEGER s }, 70-72 bytes
rsa_pss_rsae_sha256    -> exactly the modulus size, 256 bytes for RSA-2048

27.request: CertificateVerify proves possession of the certificate's private key over the transcript up to Certificate.
27.response: Finished proves possession of the handshake traffic secret — that is, of the (EC)DHE shared secret — over the transcript up to CertificateVerify.

28.note: Two Finished messages, two different finished keys, two different transcripts. The client's covers the server's, so it can only be produced after it.

28.request: A Finished whose verify_data is anything other than HMAC(client finished_key, Transcript-Hash(CH..server Finished))

34.request: One side has finished writing and says so

37.title: Which alert for which kind of broken
37.request:
A type that does not exist         -> unexpected_message(10)
A body that will not parse         -> decode_error(50)
A body that parses but is illegal  -> illegal_parameter(47)
A length longer than the bytes sent -> wait, then decode_error
37.response: All of them fatal, all of them closing the connection. The distinction is for the operator reading a log, not for the peer.

38.title: What replaced renegotiation
38.request: TLS 1.2 used renegotiation for three things: rekeying, client authentication after the fact, and changing parameters mid-connection.

7.title: An abandoned handshake
7.request: The client sends a ClientHello, reads the ServerHello, and then simply stops — no Finished, no close_notify, the socket left open.
7.response: Nothing, until the server's own timeout. What matters is that the server is still accepting new connections while it waits.
7.note: This is what a port scanner and a flaky mobile client both look like. A server that blocks its accept loop on one half-finished handshake is trivially denied service by a single connection.

8.title: Where the version really lives
8.request: legacy_version 0x0303, and a supported_versions extension whose list holds 0x0304
8.response: legacy_version 0x0303 again, and a supported_versions extension holding the two bytes 0x0304.
8.note: Both messages say 0x0303 in the field called `version`, and neither of them means it. Negotiate from the extension; the field is there so a 1990s middlebox does not panic.

8.title: The two shapes of supported_versions
8.request: ClientHello: extension_data is a one-byte count followed by that many uint16 versions — `02 03 04` for a 1.3-only client.
8.response: ServerHello: extension_data is a bare uint16 — `03 04`. No list, no count.
8.note: The same extension code point, two different bodies, depending on which message it is in. That asymmetry is real and it is easy to miss.

9.title: A hello that offers only TLS 1.2
9.request: A normal-looking ClientHello whose supported_versions list holds 0x0303 and nothing else
9.response: An alert record: level fatal(2), description protocol_version(70), sent in the clear because no keys exist yet. Then the connection closes.
9.note: Two bytes in the alert record's fragment, `02 46`. That is the whole message — there is nothing else a 1.3-only server can say to a 1.2-only client.
